paras: The lynching of William and Bradford Courts took place at Brookville, Bracken County, Kentucky, on the night of April 26, 1882, when a mob took the two brothers from the jail and hanged them from a tree.
The brothers were being held over the killing of James Smith in a quarrel near Fairview a few days earlier.
The story ran as a wire item across the country, often in roundups of several lynchings reported the same day.

According to a dispatch from Augusta, Kentucky, to the Cincinnati Commercial, the Courts brothers quarreled with James and John Smith on the Saturday before, at a log-rolling near Fairview. The Wheeling Intelligencer's version of the dispatch said the dispute was "about the shooting of Mrs. Smith's cow." Bradford Courts was said to have killed James Smith with a pistol and escaped, though one brief said both brothers "shot and killed" Smith.

Officers and citizens followed him to the Courts house, where they reported finding "a large quantity of stolen goods" and Bradford hidden under the floor beneath a trap door. Both brothers were taken to the jail at Brookville on Monday to await an examination.

On the night before the examination, a mob took the keys from the jailer, or by another account overpowered him, and removed the prisoners. The brothers were carried about half a mile from the jail and hanged together, "side by side," from the limb of a tree. No report names anyone in the mob or gives its size; a New Jersey digest described "a crowd of armed men."
No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage. In December a year-end chronology still listed "two at Brookville Ky." among the murderers lynched on April 27.

The first reports appeared on April 28 in the New-York Tribune, the Wheeling Intelligencer and the Portland Daily Press, all from the Cincinnati dispatch; the Portland item placed the town in Georgia. Headlines such as "Two Brothers Lynched in Kentucky" and "Hanged by a Mob" ran over the wire account, which called the brothers "desperadoes" and Bradford "a young rough."

Kentucky papers ran it as a short state item; the Stanford Interior Journal called the brothers "disreputable characters," and the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian spelled the town "Brooksville." The Bourbon News grouped the hanging with lynchings at Lake City, Colorado, and near Colusa, California, ending, "A good record for one day," a line the Somerset Press in Ohio repeated.

Through early May a short brief and a condensed telegram were reprinted in weeklies in Wisconsin, Michigan, Tennessee and Missouri. A Kansas editorial counted "two men were lynched together in Kentucky" among recent cases and argued that a victim's deserving hanging did not justify a mob. No report gave a race for the Courts brothers, while the same columns marked Black people as "colored."

Reports give the brothers' ages as seventeen and twenty-four or as nineteen and twenty-four. The date also varies: the Cincinnati dispatch of April 27 said "last night" and a condensed telegram said "the night of the 26th," while roundups gave "the 27th."

bases: A mob took the two brothers from the Brookville jail and hanged them from a tree while they awaited examination on a murder charge (A1, A9, A13).

A 'mob' or 'crowd of armed men' took both brothers from jail and hanged them for the killing of James Smith, before any examination (A1, A9, A14). No report gives a race for the brothers, and the papers do not present it as a racial case.
The Commercial's Augusta special (A1, A3), a separate Fairview wire (A4), a condensed telegram (A9) and Kentucky state-news columns (A6, A7) agree on the jail seizure and double hanging.
